resolvedIdentity: Tune's continuous church site on the ra ridge, physically anchored to the standing 1910 church and historically layered with the medieval church, the 1865 church and the Tune runestone find context.

coordinateDecision.reason: The legacy point was about three kilometres west of the site. The applied point is the named standing church geometry and matches the independent church entity, address and heritage identifiers.

sources.name: Church of Norway – Tune kirke
findings: A church at the site is mentioned in 1080 and the surrounding cemetery is registered as medieval.
The medieval church was demolished in 1863.
The present church was consecrated on 30 December 1910 and reused parts of the 1865 walls.

sources.name: Norges Kirker – Tune kirke
findings: Tune was a county church in medieval Vingulmork.
The cemetery has been expanded but preserves the continuous kirkested context.
The Tune runestone was associated with the cemetery wall and later held by the University collection.

sources.name: Store norske leksikon – Tunesteinen
findings: The stone carries one of the longest preserved Elder Futhark inscriptions and dates to the early centuries CE.
In 1627 it stood in the churchyard wall at Tune church.
The original is now in the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo.

sources.name: Sarpsborg municipality – Tunesteinen
findings: The stone was documented in the churchyard wall in 1627 and later transported to Christiania.

sources.name: Pilegrimsleden – Tune kirke
findings: Tune church is an interest point on Borgleden in an older central power landscape.
